{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would provider-reported MMLU and GPQA figures fail the positive control that the same benchmarks pass when re-measured by the harness?", "answer": "Provider numbers come from different prompts, shot counts and decoding settings. {"id": "q27", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the harmonized MMLU/GPQA anchors had also failed the positive control, which of the paper's recommendations and analyses would lose support?", "answer": "The recommendation to fix capability by re-measuring under a uniform protocol would lose its supporting evidence. {"id": "q28", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the column-permuted score matrices had produced first eigenvalues above the parallel-analysis threshold of 2.18, which analysis would lose its warrant?", "answer": "The PCA of cross-benchmark structure on the n=18 panel would lose its warrant. {"id": "q30", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If blind coders had overwhelmingly assigned AgentHarm to 'risk recognition' rather than 'harm blocking', which part of the paper's framing would lose support?", "answer": "The §3.2 target assignments, which treat AgentHarm as the harm-blocking instrument, would lose support. {"id": "q31", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the misalignment outcome's blackmail and leaking halves had agreed with Spearman–Brown about 0.97, which characterization in the paper would change?", "answer": "The misalignment probe would no longer be one of the weakest components. {"id": "q32", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If within-model SEs had been comparable to between-model SDs rather than 13–25% of them, which of the paper's interpretive claims would fail?", "answer": "The claim that the observed panel-level spread reflects real model differences, being 4–8× the worst-case SE, would fail. {"id": "q33", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that AgentHarm is the best general predictor of agent safety? {"id": "q34", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper's high internal consistency (split-half ≥0.96) show that the audited benchmarks validly measure agent safety? {"id": "q36", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the capability–misalignment relationship disappears for 2026 models? {"id": "q37", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that every pairwise MMLU difference between panel models is reliable? {"id": "q38", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that InjecAgent and AgentDojo, both injection benchmarks, rank models consistently? {"id": "q39", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the blind coding (27/28 agreement, α=0.825) show that the authors' two-construct scheme is the correct way to categorize these benchmarks? Internal consistency shows the score is stable, not that it reflects discrimination, so specificity needs to be read together with recall or balanced accuracy.", "rubric": ["Identifies a disposition to rarely flag traces (or to label most traces benign) as the failing case.", "Explains that such a disposition yields consistently high specificity without discrimination, because consistency measures stability rather than validity, or because unsafe traces are missed."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose a revised R-Judge release changed the proportion of unsafe records. Would official F1 scores from the old and new releases be directly comparable, and why?", "answer": "No. F1 combines recall with precision and ignores true negatives, and precision depends on how many benign traces there are to falsely flag. F1 therefore shifts with the base rate even if model behavior is unchanged. Balanced accuracy weights the two classes equally regardless of base rate, which is why the paper records it alongside F1.", "rubric": ["Concludes that F1 would not be directly comparable across releases with different base rates.", "Explains that F1 depends on the class mix through precision (it ignores true negatives), whereas balanced accuracy is base-rate invariant."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The 2026 expansion excluded models only on harness telemetry, never on outcome scores. Could the expanded-panel capability–safety estimates still be biased by which models were excluded, and why?", "answer": "Yes. Gating blind to scores prevents selecting models on their outcomes, but it does not make the exclusions random. Kimi-K2.6, the Nemotron-3 models, MiniMax-M3, Gemini-2.5-Pro and GLM-4.5 dropped out for unbounded reasoning traces, low anchor usability, truncation or routing incompatibilities, so the panel underrepresents certain kinds of newer models. This mirrors the non-random coverage loss on non-standard tool interfaces in the original panel.", "rubric": ["Concludes that bias from exclusions remains possible.", "Explains that telemetry-based exclusions are non-random: they fall on particular kinds of newer models (unbounded reasoning, truncation, routing issues, a stale harness), so the panel is not representative."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The organization-histogram-matched size-21 subsets are meant to separate changes in organizational composition from changes within organizations. Would they also hold release date and capability fixed, and why?", "answer": "No. They match only the count of models per organization. Organization is only partly collinear with release date and capability, and a matched subset can include 2026 models from the same organizations that differ in date and capability. Differences between the matched subsets and the original panel can therefore still reflect those factors.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the matched subsets do not control for release date or capability.", "Explains that matching fixes only the organization histogram, while models within an organization (including 2026 models) differ in date and capability."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper finds that, against τ² task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability. Under what conditions of the τ² outcome itself would this null fail to show that the safety scores lack incremental information?", "answer": "The null is weak evidence because τ² is a single run of 40 tasks whose user-simulator variance cannot be bounded. It is also collected on only 20 models, where only correlations of about ρ=0.6 or larger are detectable with 80% power. Unbounded outcome noise and low power could both hide a moderate incremental association.", "rubric": ["States that the null may reflect the outcome's limits rather than a true absence of incremental information.", "Cites the single run with unbounded user-simulator variance and/or the low power at n=20 (minimum detectable effect around 0.6)."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the misalignment outcome's worst-case within-model SE (5.0) more than twice MMLU's (2.2), even though both are binomial SEs?", "answer": "Binomial SE shrinks as the number of scored units grows. The misalignment SE is computed over only 100 decisions per model, while MMLU's is computed over 500 fixed items, so per-model misalignment scores are estimated less precisely.", "rubric": ["Attributes the difference to the number of units: 100 decisions versus 500 items.", "Notes that binomial SE decreases as the number of units increases."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "R-Judge is run on its full 571 records. Why does its consistency row in Table 3 use 570 items?", "answer": "The split-half and bootstrap splits are shared across models and restricted to items present in every model's logs. At least one record must be missing or unusable in at least one model's logs, which leaves 570 common items.", "rubric": ["States that the analysis uses only items common to every model's logs.", "Infers that at least one record is missing for at least one model, reducing 571 to 570."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The misalignment outcome covers 21 models on the original panel. Why is the paired τ²/misalignment panel 20?", "answer": "τ² covers only 20 models because it is a multi-turn tool loop, while misalignment covers 21. The paired panel is their intersection, so it is limited by τ² coverage, and all 20 τ² models also have misalignment scores.", "rubric": ["States that the paired panel is the intersection of the two outcomes' coverage.", "Identifies τ² coverage (n=20) as the limiting factor."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the original-panel interaction test need leave-one-organization-out recomputation in addition to leave-one-model-out?", "answer": "OpenAI contributes 6 of the 22 original models, and models from one organization share training pipelines and safety tuning. Dropping one model at a time leaves the other five, so an effect shared across a developer would survive leave-one-model-out. Only removing the whole organization tests whether that developer drives the estimate.", "rubric": ["Explains that same-organization models share a common effect through shared pipelines or tuning, so leave-one-model-out cannot remove it.", "Notes the unequal contributions, for example OpenAI's 6 of 22 models, which make a single developer potentially dominant."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "An independent grader reproduces the misalignment outcome's model-level scores closely. Why does that check not resolve the paper's concern that misalignment is a weak link?", "answer": "The grader swap addresses only scoring dependence. The weakness lies in scenario sampling: the blackmail and leaking halves agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70), so scores depend on which scenario is administered. A second grader re-scores the same decisions and cannot address that.", "rubric": ["States that the grader check addresses classifier or scoring dependence only.", "Identifies the weakness as scenario dependence: the two scenario halves agree only moderately (SB 0.70)."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does it matter that the capability composite averages standardized rather than raw MMLU and GPQA scores?", "answer": "The two anchors spread models very differently: the between-model SD is 8.7 for MMLU and 18.2 for GPQA. A raw average would weight GPQA about twice as heavily in determining model differences. Standardizing gives each anchor equal weight.", "rubric": ["States that a raw average would let GPQA dominate the composite.", "Cites GPQA's roughly twice-larger between-model spread (SD 18.2 vs 8.7) and notes that standardizing equalizes the weights."]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Under AIM alone, 11 of 22 models refuse every request. Why can the three-template average separate those 11 models?", "answer": "No model sits at the ceiling under the average, so each of the 11 must show at least some harmful compliance under refusal suppression or prefix injection. Those differing amounts of compliance break the ties that AIM alone leaves.", "rubric": ["Infers that each AIM-ceiling model complies to some extent under at least one of the other two templates.", "Explains that these differing compliance levels are what break the ties."]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Prior work reports rank concordance near 0.10 across four agent-safety benchmarks on twelve models. Given this paper's power analysis, can that result distinguish benchmarks that are unrelated from benchmarks that are moderately related, and why?", "answer": "No. Even at n=18 the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is about ρ=0.62, and detecting ρ≈0.4 needs about 40 models. At 12 models, a true moderate correlation could easily yield an estimate near 0.10, and the panel sits at the paper's 'about a dozen' threshold for interpreting rank correlations at all.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the result cannot distinguish no relation from a moderate relation.", "Cites low power: minimum detectable effect about 0.62 at n=18 (worse at 12) and about 40 models needed for ρ≈0.4."]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team will build a shortlist of the safest quarter of models and wants it to be robust to which items happened to be sampled. Based on Table 3, would a shortlist drawn from AgentHarm or from the jailbreak outcome be more robust, and why?", "answer": "The jailbreak outcome. {"id": "q17", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A new reasoning model produces unstable long-form chain-of-thought on GPQA-Diamond. Following the paper's precedent, what is its status in the capability-adjusted analyses versus the chat-based outcome data?", "answer": "Like DeepSeek-R1, it would be excluded from the anchor panel, so it cannot enter capability-composite or rank-residualized analyses. It can still be scored on chat-based outcomes such as the jailbreak suite and included in their internal-consistency analysis, as DeepSeek-R1 was (42 models in Table 3).", "rubric": ["States that it is excluded from the anchors and therefore from capability-adjusted analyses.", "States that it can still be scored on, and included in the consistency analysis of, chat-based outcomes such as the jailbreak suite (the DeepSeek-R1 precedent)."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team argues that R-Judge is not capability-confounded because R-Judge specificity barely correlates with the capability composite. Per the paper, which other R-Judge summary must they examine before making that claim, and why?", "answer": "They should examine recall, and also F1 and balanced accuracy, which mix recall in. Recall rewards detecting unsafe content, which presupposes comprehension. Specificity can be achieved by a disposition to flag rarely. Capability content is a property of each summary, so a null on specificity does not transfer to the benchmark as a whole.", "rubric": ["Names recall (or the recall-containing summaries F1 and balanced accuracy).", "Explains that recall presupposes comprehension, while specificity can come from a disposition to flag rarely, so capability content is metric-specific."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to strengthen the misalignment outcome. Per the paper, should they collect more decisions within the existing blackmail and leaking scenarios or add scenarios, and why?", "answer": "They should add scenarios, along with replicate runs. The instrument's weakness is scenario dependence: the two halves agree only at Spearman–Brown 0.70. More decisions within the same two scenarios would shrink the binomial SE but would not address variation across scenarios. New scenarios should be pre-specified and should keep the probe specific to autonomous-agent misbehavior, unlike the severe-harm murder scenario.", "rubric": ["Recommends adding scenarios (or replicates across scenarios) rather than only more decisions within the existing two.", "Explains that the weakness is moderate cross-scenario agreement (SB 0.70), which within-scenario decisions do not address."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A new safety benchmark is scored by a multi-stage LLM-judge pipeline. Following the lesson of the paper's judge swaps, how should its judge-robustness check be designed?", "answer": "The check should re-run the full grading pipeline with a different judge rather than swapping only one component. The AgentHarm swap re-did only the refusal component and agreed less closely than the full-judge swaps on the misalignment and jailbreak outcomes, which reproduced model-level scores closely.", "rubric": ["Recommends swapping or re-running the entire grading pipeline, not a single stage.", "Cites the AgentHarm refusal-only swap agreeing less closely than the full swaps on misalignment and jailbreak."]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If XSTest's unsafe subset had shown wide spread across models instead of 83–100% refusal (sd 4.5), which argument in the paper would lose force?", "answer": "The paper argues that overtly harmful single-turn prompts no longer separate current models, which is one reason agentic and jailbreak-based instruments are needed. A discriminating unsafe subset would undercut that motivation and would make the unsafe subset, not only the safe-subset over-refusal, informative.", "rubric": ["Identifies the argument that single-turn harmful prompts no longer separate models, so agentic or jailbreak instruments are needed.", "Explains that a discriminating unsafe subset would contradict the ceiling on which that argument rests."]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If R-Judge specificity had shown low split-half consistency, around 0.5, instead of 0.99, which recommendation of the paper would be weakened, and why?", "answer": "The recommendation to report specificity alongside F1 as the complementary summary of the benign-trace error type would be weakened. If specificity were largely item-sampling noise, re-summarizing R-Judge under specificity (or a metric including it) would not reliably rank models for a monitor with costly false alarms.", "rubric": ["Identifies the recommendation to report specificity (or full confusion-matrix complements) alongside F1.", "Explains that an unreliable specificity would make specificity-based rankings mostly item-sampling noise."]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the 2,000-panel calibration check had shown the organization permutation test rejecting about 15% of the time at α=0.05 under the standard nulls, which analysis would lose its warrant?", "answer": "The organization-group comparison on the expanded panel would lose its warrant, because its p-values would overstate evidence of between-organization differences. The paper's statement that the test is adequately calibrated for panels of this shape would no longer hold.", "rubric": ["Identifies the organization-group permutation comparison (or its calibration claim).", "Explains that inflated Type-I error would make its significance overstate organization differences."]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If AgentHarm had shown the weakest rather than the strongest held-out association with the jailbreak outcome, which interpretation would be challenged, and why?", "answer": "The paper reads the AgentHarm–jailbreak link as agreement between two instruments that both score harmful compliance. Weak agreement between two instruments aimed at a similar behavior would cast doubt on whether they measure that behavior consistently. It would point to a measurement problem, such as AgentHarm's grading or the jailbreak templates, rather than confirming convergence.", "rubric": ["Identifies the reading of the association as agreement between two harmful-compliance instruments.", "Explains that weak agreement between instruments aimed at the same behavior would suggest a measurement problem rather than convergence."]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the second misalignment grader (Claude-3-Haiku vs GPT-4o) had disagreed strongly at the model level, which conclusions would lose support?", "answer": "The claim that the misalignment outcome is not an artifact of a particular classifier would fail. Consequently, the capability–misalignment associations, both the original opposite association and its weakening on the expanded panel, could reflect the classifier rather than model behavior.", "rubric": ["Identifies the claim that misalignment scores are robust to classifier or grader choice.", "Notes that the capability–misalignment findings (original or expanded) would then be classifier-dependent."]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the harness had retained only each model's official R-Judge F1 rather than per-model verdicts and labels, which parts of the paper's analyses could not have been produced?", "answer": "Specificity, recall and balanced accuracy could not be computed, nor the constant-verdict reference rows. The R-Judge specificity row in Table 3 and the split-half and bootstrap analyses of R-Judge, which need item-level verdicts, would also be impossible, as would recomputing R-Judge quantities under alternative metrics.", "rubric": ["Names the alternative metrics (specificity, recall, balanced accuracy) and/or the constant-verdict reference rows.", "Notes that the item-level consistency analyses for R-Judge (Table 3 rows) also depend on stored per-item verdicts."]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that R-Judge scores are unrelated to the misalignment outcome? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The pre-specified continuation on an intermediate n=25 panel did not meet its threshold and was stopped. At that size, moderate correlations such as ρ≈0.4 (which need about 40 models) are not reliably detectable, so the paper keeps the relationship only as a hypothesis.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Cites the stopped n=25 continuation together with low power (about 40 models needed for ρ≈0.4), so failure to meet the threshold is not evidence of no relation."]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that high capability ensures jailbreak safety among current models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. On the expanded panel, jailbreak safety among high-capability models spans most of the scale. Capable models can therefore be either robust or highly vulnerable to the templates.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted.", "Cites that jailbreak safety among high-capability models spans most of the scale on the expanded panel."]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the audited agent-safety benchmarks share a single latent factor? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The PCA on 18 models and six columns is treated as a description of the sample, not a model of latent structure. Its eigenvalues are uncertain, and Pearson and Spearman conventions can retain different numbers of components. The passing negative control only shows that the pipeline does not create structure from noise.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Cites at least one of: small n=18 with limited resolution, convention sensitivity, the PCA being descriptive only, or the negative control testing only noise."]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its jailbreak outcome would rank models the same way under a different set of published jailbreak templates? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Only AIM, refusal suppression and prefix injection were used. Robustness checks covered base-prompt resampling and judge swaps, not template choice, and the AIM-only ceiling shows that template choice can change results substantially. Per-template scores are stored only so that such analyses can be run later.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Notes that only three templates were tested, robustness checks did not vary templates, and/or the AIM ceiling shows results are template-sensitive."]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that R-Judge's official F1 should be abandoned in favor of specificity? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. The paper recommends reporting complementary metrics and constant-verdict reference rows alongside F1, not replacing it. The appropriate summary depends on the use case: a monitor with costly false alarms should prefer one that includes specificity, while a last-line filter may prefer recall.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted (or not supported).", "Explains that the paper recommends reporting alternatives alongside F1, with metric choice depending on use case, such as recall for a last-line filter."]},
{"id": "q32", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its capability-adjusted correlations are insensitive to the choice between re-ranking rank residuals and taking Pearson correlations on unre-ranked rank residuals? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper states only that the two conventions coincide in large samples and differ slightly in small ones. It implements both so readers can check, but it reports no comparison showing that conclusions on its small panels are unchanged.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Notes that the conventions differ in small samples and that both are implemented, but no result establishing insensitivity is reported."]},
{"id": "q33", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p1", "question": "A model has flagged some benign R-Judge traces. Extra benign traces are added to the dataset, and the model correctly passes all of them, with its other verdicts unchanged. Would its official F1 change?", "answer": "No. F1 combines recall and precision, and true negatives enter neither. Adding correctly passed benign traces adds only true negatives, so F1 is unchanged.", "rubric": ["Answers no, F1 does not change.", "Explains that the added traces are true negatives, which F1 ignores (recall and precision are unchanged)."]},
{"id": "q34", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p1", "question": "A model has flagged some benign R-Judge traces. Extra benign traces are added to the dataset, and the model correctly passes all of them, with its other verdicts unchanged. Would its balanced accuracy change?", "answer": "Yes, it would rise. Specificity, the fraction of benign traces correctly passed, increases when more benign traces are passed while the existing false positives stay fixed. Balanced accuracy averages specificity with performance on unsafe traces.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, balanced accuracy increases.", "Explains that specificity rises because true negatives increase while false positives are fixed, and balanced accuracy includes specificity."]},
{"id": "q35", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under the paper's pre-specified rule, would the common-panel PCA be interpreted if the capability anchors were the provider-reported MMLU and GPQA figures?", "answer": "No. The PCA is interpreted only if the positive and negative controls pass, and the positive control fails on provider-reported anchors.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Cites the rule that the PCA is interpreted only if the controls pass, together with the positive-control failure on provider numbers."]},
{"id": "q36", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under the paper's pre-specified rule, would the common-panel PCA be interpreted using the harmonized MMLU and GPQA anchors?", "answer": "Yes, as a descriptive summary of the sample. {"id": "q37", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could the 2026 expansion data be used to update the correlation between capability and jailbreak safety?", "answer": "Yes. The expansion re-measured both capability anchors and the jailbreak outcome under the original protocol on 41 anchored models.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Notes that both the anchors and the jailbreak outcome were collected for the new models."]},
{"id": "q38", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could the 2026 expansion data be used to update the correlation between InjecAgent robustness and misalignment safety?", "answer": "No. The new models skipped the tool-calling audit benchmarks, and InjecAgent ran only on the original panel. {"id": "q39", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Could InjecAgent robustness scores shift if the judge model used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?", "answer": "No. InjecAgent is rule-scored, so no judge model enters its scoring.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Explains that InjecAgent is rule-scored, with no judge model."]},
{"id": "q40", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Could AgentHarm safety scores shift if its judge were replaced with a different LLM judge?", "answer": "Yes. AgentHarm is graded through a pipeline with a gpt-4o-mini judge, and re-scoring its refusal component with a Gemini judge agreed less closely than the judge swaps on the other outcomes.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Cites AgentHarm's LLM-judge grading and the less close agreement of the refusal-judge swap."]}
]}

{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Under what kind of model-specific problem could the harmonized anchors pass the positive control and still give that model a misleading capability composite, and why?", "answer": "A model-specific harness or parsing problem that depresses both MMLU and GPQA together, because both anchors run through the same API harness. Why is this reassuring rather than a sign of spurious structure?", "answer": "The threshold is the 95th percentile of the random-normal null, so about 5% of structure-free matrices would be expected to exceed it by chance. An exceedance of 2%, with a median first eigenvalue of 1.71 against 2.18, is no higher than chance, so the pipeline is not creating structure from noise.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the 2% exceedance is consistent with no spurious structure", "Explains that the threshold is a 95th-percentile null value, so roughly 5% exceedance is expected by chance and 2% does not exceed that"]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would adding AgentDojo as a column in the common-panel PCA make the analysis worse rather than more complete?", "answer": "The PCA needs every model to have a score on every column. AgentDojo covers only 5 models, so the shared set would fall from 18 to at most 5. That is far below the roughly a dozen models the paper requires before interpreting rank relationships.", "rubric": ["States that including AgentDojo would shrink the analyzable panel to at most 5 models", "Links this to the need for complete rows across columns and the paper's minimum of about a dozen models"]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "GLM-4.5 produced a valid MMLU score. Why can it still not enter any capability-adjusted analysis?", "answer": "The capability composite is the mean of the standardized MMLU and GPQA anchors. GLM-4.5 has no GPQA score, so no composite can be formed for it. It therefore appears only as a partial row in Figure 3.", "rubric": ["States that the model has no capability composite", "Explains that the composite requires both standardized MMLU and GPQA, and GLM-4.5 lacks GPQA"]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The pre-specified R-Judge/misalignment continuation on an n=25 intermediate panel missed its threshold. Why does the paper keep it as a hypothesis rather than treat it as evidence that no relationship exists?", "answer": "At n=25 the panel is still underpowered for moderate correlations. A ρ of about 0.4 needs roughly 40 models for 80% power, and even n=18 only detects about 0.62. Failing to reach the threshold is therefore uninformative about a moderate true relationship.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the miss does not show the absence of a relationship", "Cites low power: about 40 models are needed for ρ≈0.4, and n=25 falls well short"]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The InjecAgent–AgentDojo convergent control is inconclusive. Why does that not prevent the common-panel PCA from being interpreted under the paper's pre-specified rule?", "answer": "The rule makes PCA interpretation conditional only on the positive and negative controls, and both pass. AgentDojo is not one of the PCA columns. The inconclusive convergent control therefore leaves the condition for interpretation untouched.", "rubric": ["States that the PCA can still be interpreted", "Explains that the rule requires only the positive and negative controls to pass, both of which do, and/or that AgentDojo is not a PCA column"]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would correlating an AIM-only jailbreak score with other refusal-based instruments tend to understate any association that exists?", "answer": "Under AIM alone, 11 of 22 models refuse every request and tie at the ceiling. Whatever ordering those models have on the other instruments cannot be matched by the jailbreak scores. The tied half of the panel adds noise to the rank correlation and weakens it.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the AIM-only score would attenuate (understate) the association", "Explains that half the panel ties at the ceiling, so differences among those models cannot contribute to the rank correlation"]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper gives 0.5^4 ≈ 6.2% as the chance that one coder matches all four labels by coin flip. What is the analogous chance baseline for one coder matching all six targets in the distractor round, and why is it smaller?", "answer": "About (1/3)^6 ≈ 0.14%, because each of the six targets now has three possible constructs. With more options per target and more targets, matching every label by chance is far less likely than 6.2%, which is why the round is more demanding.", "rubric": ["Gives approximately (1/3)^6, about 0.14% (or an equivalent expression)", "Explains that three constructs per target and six targets make a chance match much less likely than in the two-construct, four-benchmark round"]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "A reader applies a Bonferroni correction to the released R-Judge analyses. What does following the paper's recommendation to report specificity, recall, balanced accuracy and F1 do to that correction, compared with reporting official F1 alone?", "answer": "It multiplies the number of R-Judge-involving tests by about four, which makes the per-test threshold stricter. The paper warns that the number of tests grows quickly with the number of metrics reported per benchmark. Reporting all four summaries is therefore a trade-off against family-wise power.", "rubric": ["States that the correction becomes stricter because the number of tests roughly quadruples", "Ties this to the paper's warning that the test count grows with the number of metrics reported per benchmark"]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Two teams analyze the same 18-model score matrix. One uses the Pearson convention, the other the Spearman convention, and they retain different numbers of components. Per the paper, does this mean one team made an error, and what should they report?", "answer": "Not necessarily. With bounded, skewed instruments and a small panel, the two conventions can legitimately retain different numbers of components. Both should be reported, and the factor analysis should be treated as supporting rather than primary evidence.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the discrepancy does not imply an error", "Explains that convention sensitivity is expected on small panels with bounded, skewed scores, so both conventions should be reported and the PCA treated as supporting evidence"]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A new organization contributes two anchored models to an expanded panel. Can it be one of the groups in the paper's permutation-test comparison of organizations, and why?", "answer": "No. The pre-specified comparison includes only organization groups with at least three models. Its two models can still appear in pooled analyses, but the organization cannot form a comparison group.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the organization cannot be a comparison group", "Cites the requirement of at least three models per organization group"]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team plans a cross-benchmark study and wants 80% power at α=0.05 to detect a true Spearman correlation of about 0.5. Based on the paper's power figures, roughly how large must its panel be?", "answer": "Larger than 18 but smaller than about 40. At n=18 the minimum detectable effect is about 0.62, above 0.5, while about 40 models are needed for 0.4. A target of 0.5 therefore needs a panel somewhere in between, in the high 20s or 30s.", "rubric": ["Gives a size between about 18 and about 40 (more than the n=18 common panel)", "Justifies this from n=18 detecting only ρ≈0.62 and ρ≈0.4 needing about 40 models"]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "After the study, a team uses the stored per-template jailbreak scores to test whether prefix injection alone predicts AgentHarm safety. How should that result be treated under the paper's practices?", "answer": "As exploratory, because the primary pre-specified outcome is the three-template average and a single-template analysis is outside the plan. The team should also check that template for ceilings, since a single template can saturate, as AIM did.", "rubric": ["States that the result is exploratory (not pre-specified) because the primary outcome is the three-template average", "Notes the need to check the single template for a ceiling effect, as with AIM"]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the harmonized capability composite had shown no association with τ² task success, which role the paper assigns to τ² would be undermined?", "answer": "Its role as the reference outcome that capability is expected to explain, against which the safety outcomes are read. If capability failed to track task success, either the composite or the τ² measurement would be suspect. Contrasting the safety outcomes with τ² would then lose its anchor.", "rubric": ["Identifies τ²'s role as the reference outcome that capability should explain", "Explains that without that association the contrast with the safety outcomes, and confidence in the composite or τ², would be undermined"]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If R-Judge specificity, recall, balanced accuracy and F1 had ordered the models identically, which of the paper's arguments would lose its practical force?", "answer": "The argument that metric choice is part of the claim: that R-Judge's capability content differs by summary and secondary analyses should report the alternatives. If all summaries gave the same ranking, the choice of summary would not change conclusions in practice.", "rubric": ["Identifies the argument that capability content and conclusions depend on which R-Judge summary is used (metric choice is part of the claim)", "Explains that identical rankings would leave no case in which the summary choice changes conclusions"]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the impressions formed on the first seven-model panel had held up on the full n=18 common panel, which recommendation would lose its first-hand motivating evidence?", "answer": "The recommendation to treat small-panel relationships as provisional, show subsampling variability and avoid interpreting rank correlations on fewer than about a dozen models. The authors' own failed n=7 impressions are their direct example of the hazard.", "rubric": ["Identifies the recommendation to treat small-panel correlations as provisional, report subsampling variability, and avoid interpreting fewer than about a dozen models", "Explains that the non-persistence of the n=7 impressions is the paper's first-hand demonstration of that hazard"]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the harness had measured only one capability anchor (say MMLU), which of the pre-specified harness controls could not have been run at all?", "answer": "The positive control, because it is defined as the capability anchors agreeing with one another. With a single anchor there is no second measure to agree with, so the comparison between provider-reported and harmonized anchors on this control could not have been made.", "rubric": ["Identifies the positive control", "Explains that it requires agreement between two anchors, which is impossible with only one"]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Per-model SEs for the jailbreak outcome are reported to be small. If its top-quartile persistence had nonetheless come out low, which statement in the paper would that illustrate?", "answer": "That small SEs do not by themselves make rankings stable, which is the stated reason internal consistency is computed in addition to precision. Precise per-model scores can still give a top group that reshuffles under item resampling when models are close.", "rubric": ["Identifies the statement that small SEs alone do not guarantee stable rankings (the motivation for the consistency analyses)", "Explains that rankings can reshuffle under item resampling even when individual scores are precise"]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does Table 3 show that every item-rich instrument has an uncorrected split-half correlation of at least 0.96? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Only R-Judge specificity reaches 0.98 uncorrected; the others are 0.93–0.95. The ≥0.96 figure refers to Spearman–Brown corrected values, which project the consistency of the full-length instrument.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Explains that most uncorrected values are 0.93–0.95 and the ≥0.96 threshold applies to Spearman–Brown corrected values"]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that error in the capability covariate can only weaken, never inflate, its capability-adjusted relationships? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. The paper says covariate measurement error attenuates or distorts adjusted relationships in directions that are hard to sign. Adjusted estimates could therefore be biased either way, not only toward zero.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Cites the paper's statement that covariate error attenuates or distorts adjusted relationships in hard-to-sign directions"]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7", "c6", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that more capable models are, in general, more prone to agentic misalignment? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The opposite-direction association comes from the original panel and weakens on the 41-model expansion. The outcome is a single fictional-scenario probe whose halves agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70), and capability is a static composite. The claim does not generalize from this evidence.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Cites at least one of: the weakening on the expanded panel, the fictional single-scenario probe with only moderate half agreement, or the static capability composite"]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper's InjecAgent evidence establish model rankings for prompt-injection robustness in general? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. InjecAgent was run on 300 rule-scored items stratified across only the direct-harm and data-stealing categories. Its convergent check against AgentDojo is inconclusive at n=5. High internal consistency shows stable rankings on these items, not across injection types generally.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Cites the restricted item set (direct-harm and data-stealing items) and/or the inconclusive convergent control, noting that internal consistency covers only this item set"]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that current models no longer differ in how they refuse harmful requests? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Only the XSTest unsafe subset of overtly harmful prompts is ceilinged (83–100%). Under the three-template jailbreak suite, safety among high-capability expanded-panel models spans most of the scale, so models still differ under jailbreak pressure.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Contrasts the ceilinged overtly-harmful XSTest subset with the wide spread on the three-template jailbreak outcome"]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that BFCL is an invalid benchmark of function-calling ability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper reports only a six-model pilot showing that BFCL failed as an agentic replacement for the capability covariate, apparently rewarding format conformance. That is a narrow finding about its use as a covariate on this panel, not a general verdict on the benchmark.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the evidence is a six-model pilot about its suitability as a capability covariate (format conformance), not a general validity test"]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": "p1", "question": "An organization-group permutation test on the misalignment outcome gives p≈0.04. Is this result exposed to the false-positive inflation found under the worst-case clustered-variance null?", "answer": "No. The worst-case inflation appeared on the jailbreak structure only. Rejection rates for misalignment matched nominal α (0.045–0.052 at α=0.05).", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Notes that the worst-case inflation was found only on the jailbreak structure, with misalignment calibrated at nominal levels"]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": "p1", "question": "An organization-group permutation test on the jailbreak outcome gives p≈0.04. Is this result exposed to the false-positive inflation found under the worst-case clustered-variance null?", "answer": "Yes, to a mild degree. Under the worst-case null the jailbreak test rejects about 6.7% of the time at α=0.05, so a result near 0.05 is less secure. Only at α=0.005 was no inflation detected.", "rubric": ["Answers yes (mildly)", "Cites the 0.067 rejection rate at α=0.05 on jailbreak, with no inflation only at the stricter α=0.005"]},
{"id": "q32", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c8"], "pair": "p2", "question": "An agent appears injection-robust only because it rarely completes any requested task. Would AgentDojo's scoring expose this?", "answer": "Yes. AgentDojo is environment-scored for utility as well as security, so an agent that does little would show low utility alongside its high security.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that AgentDojo scores utility as well as security"]},
{"id": "q33", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c8"], "pair": "p2", "question": "An agent appears injection-robust only because it rarely completes any requested task. Would InjecAgent's robustness score expose this?", "answer": "No. InjecAgent robustness is rule-scored as one minus attack success and has no utility component. An agent that rarely acts would simply show low attack success and look robust.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that InjecAgent scores only attack success (robustness = 1 − attack success), with no utility measure"]},
{"id": "q34", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Would running each model on τ²-retail several more times allow a within-model uncertainty bound to be placed on its τ² score?", "answer": "Yes. The missing bound comes from user-simulator variance, which a single run cannot capture. Replicate runs would expose run-to-run variation from which an SE could be estimated.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that the obstacle is user-simulator variance across runs, which replicate runs make observable"]},
{"id": "q35", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Would re-scoring each model's existing τ²-retail final database states a second time allow a within-model uncertainty bound to be placed on its τ² score?", "answer": "No. τ² success is environment-scored from the final database state and does not depend on a judge, so re-scoring would reproduce the same result. The variance comes from the user simulator during the single run, which re-scoring cannot reveal.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that environment scoring is judge-free, so re-scoring reproduces the same result, while the unbounded variance comes from the simulator during the run"]},
{"id": "q36", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Could a model with poor comprehension of interaction traces still achieve high R-Judge specificity?", "answer": "Yes. Specificity rewards leaving benign traces alone, which a disposition to rarely flag anything achieves without understanding the traces.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that specificity can be achieved by a disposition to flag rarely, without comprehension"]},
{"id": "q37", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Could a model with poor comprehension of interaction traces still achieve high R-Judge balanced accuracy?", "answer": "No. Balanced accuracy weights benign and unsafe traces equally, so it also requires high recall on unsafe traces. Catching unsafe content without flagging everything presupposes comprehension, and a rarely-flagging disposition would score low on recall.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that balanced accuracy also requires recall on unsafe traces, which presupposes comprehension (a rarely-flagging disposition fails on recall)"]}
]}

{"items":[
{"id":"q1","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3","c8"],"pair":"p1","question":"Could models' R-Judge F1 scores shift if the gpt-4o-mini judge used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?","answer":"No. R-Judge is run as a self-judge benchmark: the score compares each model's own safe/unsafe verdict with the record's label, so no external judge model enters the scoring.","rubric":["Asserts that R-Judge F1 would not shift (no / unaffected).","Reason: R-Judge is self-judged; verdicts are compared directly against labels, with no external LLM judge in the scoring."]},
{"id":"q2","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3","c8"],"pair":"p1","question":"Could models' XSTest safe-subset over-refusal rates shift if the gpt-4o-mini judge used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?","answer":"Yes. XSTest is scored with the published CPI (compliance/partial/refusal) scorer, which uses gpt-4o-mini as its judge. Changing the judge can change which responses count as refusals.","rubric":["Asserts that the rates could shift (yes).","Reason: XSTest's CPI scorer relies on a gpt-4o-mini judge to classify responses as compliance, partial or refusal."]},
{"id":"q3","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1","c7","c4"],"pair":"p2","question":"Suppose Gemini-2.5-Pro, which yielded no valid capability anchor, had nonetheless had its jailbreak responses fully judged. Could it be included in the jailbreak row of the internal-consistency table (Table 3)?","answer":"Yes. The consistency computation needs only item-level jailbreak data, not anchors. The paper already includes DeepSeek-R1, which lacks the anchor pair, which is why that row has 42 models. Gemini-2.5-Pro would need judged responses on the shared base prompts so that the common prompt set does not shrink.","rubric":["Asserts yes, it could be included.","Reason: internal consistency uses only the instrument's item-level data, and DeepSeek-R1 was included without an anchor pair (42 models).","Condition: its judged prompts must cover the shared prompt set, or the intersection would shrink."]},
{"id":"q4","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1","c7","c4"],"pair":"p2","question":"Under the same supposition (Gemini-2.5-Pro jailbreak responses fully judged, no valid anchor), could Gemini-2.5-Pro enter the expanded-panel correlation between capability and jailbreak safety?","answer":"No. That analysis uses the 41 anchored models and needs each model's harmonized capability composite. A model with no valid MMLU/GPQA anchor has no composite, so it cannot be placed on the capability axis.","rubric":["Asserts no.","Reason: capability analyses require the harmonized anchor composite, and the expanded analyses are restricted to anchored models; Gemini-2.5-Pro has no valid anchor."]},
{"id":"q5","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p3","question":"If MMLU were administered on 1,000 fixed items instead of 500, would its worst-case within-model SE be expected to fall?","answer":"Yes. The MMLU SE is binomial, so it shrinks with the square root of the item count. The worst case would fall from about 2.2 to about 1.6 points.","rubric":["Asserts yes, the worst-case SE would fall.","Reason: a binomial SE scales with 1/sqrt(number of items), so doubling the items lowers it (to roughly 1.6 points)."]},
{"id":"q6","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p3","question":"If MMLU were administered on 1,000 fixed items instead of 500, would its between-model SD (8.7) be expected to fall correspondingly?","answer":"No. The between-model SD mainly reflects real differences in model accuracy, which more items do not remove; only the small item-noise component would shrink. The SE-to-SD ratio would therefore improve.","rubric":["Asserts no, the between-model SD would not fall correspondingly (it would stay roughly the same).","Reason: the SD reflects true spread among models rather than item-sampling noise, so only the SE shrinks and the SE/SD ratio improves."]},
{"id":"q7","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p4","question":"In the PCA negative control, if each score column is permuted independently across models, does the permutation destroy any between-column correlation present in the real data?","answer":"Yes. Shuffling each column separately breaks the link between a model's score on one instrument and its scores on the others. Any real covariance structure is removed, which is what makes the result a null against which to check the pipeline.","rubric":["Asserts yes.","Reason: independent shuffling of each column decouples models' scores across instruments, so any genuine correlation structure is removed and the result is a valid null."]},
{"id":"q8","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p4","question":"If instead the same reordering of models were applied to every column jointly, would the permutation destroy any between-column correlation present in the real data?","answer":"No. A joint permutation only relabels the rows. Each model keeps its full set of scores, so the correlation matrix and its eigenvalues are identical to the real data's, and the result cannot serve as a null.","rubric":["Asserts no.","Reason: applying one permutation to all columns just reorders models while keeping each model's scores together, so the correlations and eigenvalues are unchanged."]},
{"id":"q9","type":"why","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the paper run its organization-group analysis (permutation test over organizations with at least three models) only on the expanded panel and not on the original 22-model roster?","answer":"On the original roster only four organizations have three or more models (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3), and only OpenAI has four or more. The other five organizations contribute one or two models each. That leaves too few clusters and too few models per cluster for a group comparison. The expanded panel has seven organizations with three or more models and six with four or more.","rubric":["Concludes that the original roster has too few organizations with enough models for the group comparison.","Reason: only four original organizations reach three models (OpenAI 6, Meta, Qwen, Mistral 3) and only OpenAI reaches four, whereas the expanded panel has seven with three or more and six with four or more."]},
{"id":"q10","type":"why","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Why are both the median first eigenvalue of the column-permuted matrices (1.71) and the parallel-analysis threshold (2.18) well above 1, even though the permuted columns are unrelated by construction?","answer":"With only 18 models and six columns, sampling noise alone produces sizeable chance correlations among unrelated columns. The largest eigenvalue of such data therefore lands well above 1. This is why the paper compares eigenvalues with a simulated random-normal null rather than with a fixed cutoff, and why it notes that eigenvalues on this panel carry substantial sampling uncertainty.","rubric":["Concludes that eigenvalues above 1 are expected even for unrelated columns.","Reason: with small n (18 models), chance correlations from sampling noise inflate the largest eigenvalue, which is why a simulated parallel-analysis null is used instead of a fixed threshold."]},
{"id":"q11","type":"why","claims":["c2","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"GPQA's median within-model SE (3.3) is close to its maximum (3.6), while MMLU's median (1.6) is well below its maximum (2.2). Why the difference, given that both are binomial SEs?","answer":"A binomial SE peaks when accuracy is near 50%; 2.2 and 3.6 are roughly the maxima for 500 and 198 items. A median close to the maximum means most models score in the mid range on GPQA. MMLU's much lower median means most models score far from 50%, at high accuracy, with only a few near the middle.","rubric":["Concludes that most models sit near mid-range accuracy on GPQA but well above it on MMLU.","Reason: a binomial SE is largest at about 50% accuracy and smaller toward the extremes, so the median-to-maximum gap reflects where models' accuracies fall."]},
{"id":"q12","type":"why","claims":["c5","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"The four audited benchmarks order models differently on the common panel. Why does the paper hold that this disagreement does not by itself indict any single benchmark?","answer":"Before collecting any scores, the benchmarks were assigned to different target behaviors: R-Judge and the injection benchmarks to risk recognition, and AgentHarm to harm blocking. Blinded coders recovered these assignments. Instruments aimed at different behaviors have no reason to rank models identically. What the disagreement does undercut is quoting them interchangeably as 'the safety' of an agent.","rubric":["Concludes that disagreement is expected rather than evidence that a benchmark is faulty.","Reason: the benchmarks target different behaviors (pre-specified targets that blinded coders recovered), so their rankings need not agree; what the disagreement undermines is interchangeable use of the scores."]},
{"id":"q13","type":"why","claims":["c1","c7","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"The expanded analyses use 41 anchored models, yet the MMLU row of the internal-consistency table covers 46 models. Why?","answer":"The extra rows are models that have MMLU item logs but were excluded from the anchored panel, for example DeepSeek-R1 (unstable GPQA) and GLM-4.5 (MMLU but no GPQA). Internal consistency is a property of the instrument and needs only item-level data. It does not require the full anchor pair or passing the gates needed for capability-adjusted analyses.","rubric":["Concludes that the 46 include models outside the 41-model anchored panel, such as DeepSeek-R1 and GLM-4.5, that have MMLU item logs.","Reason: consistency is computed from the instrument's own item data and does not require a complete anchor composite or inclusion in capability analyses."]},
{"id":"q14","type":"why","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"InjecAgent covers all 22 models, while AgentHarm covers 19 and AgentDojo only 5. Why?","answer":"AgentHarm and AgentDojo require native tool calling. Models whose provider interface lacks the required schema are recorded as not-run rather than forced through an emulation layer, because emulation would change the instrument. InjecAgent is rule-scored and does not depend on native tool support, so every model can be run.","rubric":["Concludes that the coverage gap comes from the native tool-calling requirement.","Reason: AgentHarm and AgentDojo need native tool use, and unsupported models are not-run rather than emulated, whereas InjecAgent has no such requirement."]},
{"id":"q15","type":"why","claims":["c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the split-half computation share each random half-split across all models, using only items common to every model's logs, rather than drawing separate splits per model?","answer":"Sharing the splits means every model's half-score rests on exactly the same items. The correlation between halves then measures whether different item subsets order the models consistently. With per-model splits, models would be scored on different items, and differences in item difficulty would mix into the comparison.","rubric":["Concludes that shared splits are needed so that the comparison is of rankings on identical items.","Reason: per-model splits would put models on different items, confounding ranking consistency with differences in item difficulty."]},
{"id":"q16","type":"failure","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"AgentHarm and XSTest are both scored with gpt-4o-mini judges. Under what condition would an association between XSTest safe-subset over-refusal and AgentHarm safety be produced by scoring rather than by model behavior, and why?","answer":"This would happen if gpt-4o-mini systematically labels some response style (for example hedged or partial answers) as refusal. A model that writes in that style would be scored as refusing on both instruments, creating shared judge variance that looks like a behavioral link. ANSWER Q3:
